claim: Planarians regenerate all body parts after injury, including the central nervous system (CNS).
source: Planarians regenerate all body parts after injury, including the central nervous system (CNS).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about planarians stated in the abstract, supported by extensive prior research in the field.

claim: The functional screen identified molecules that influence neural cell fates.
source: Our screen revealed molecules that influence neural cell fates, support the formation of a major connective hub, and promote reestablishment of chemosensory behavior.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the screen, which is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The functional screen identified molecules that support the formation of a major connective hub.
source: Our screen revealed molecules that influence neural cell fates, support the formation of a major connective hub, and promote reestablishment of chemosensory behavior.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the screen, supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The functional screen identified molecules that promote reestablishment of chemosensory behavior.
source: Our screen revealed molecules that influence neural cell fates, support the formation of a major connective hub, and promote reestablishment of chemosensory behavior.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the screen, supported by behavioral assay data in the manuscript.

claim: The screen identified genes that encode signaling molecules with roles in head regeneration.
source: We also identified genes that encode signaling molecules with roles in head regeneration, including some that are produced in a previously uncharacterized parenchymal population of cells.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, supported by experimental data showing expression patterns and RNAi phenotypes.

claim: Some signaling molecules involved in head regeneration are produced in a previously uncharacterized parenchymal population of cells.
source: We also identified genes that encode signaling molecules with roles in head regeneration, including some that are produced in a previously uncharacterized parenchymal population of cells.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by FISH data showing expression in parenchymal cells that are not muscle or stem cells.

claim: Glial cells in the planarian CNS respond to injury by repressing several transcripts.
source: Finally, we explored genes downregulated during planarian regeneration and characterized, for the first time, glial cells in the planarian CNS that respond to injury by repressing several transcripts.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by gene expression data showing downregulation of glial markers after injury.

claim: This study characterized glial cells in the planarian CNS for the first time.
source: Finally, we explored genes downregulated during planarian regeneration and characterized, for the first time, glial cells in the planarian CNS that respond to injury by repressing several transcripts.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this is the first characterization of planarian glial cells, supported by molecular and morphological data.

claim: Brain regeneration requires wound signaling and healing.
source: Brain regeneration, as a process, must occur through several interrelated steps: wound signaling and healing; production of new cells by proliferation, dedifferentiation or transdifferentiation; specification of cell lineages of the proper type(s) and ratio(s); organization of new cells in three-dimensional space; differentiation of precursors; reestablishment of connections required for functional restoration; and, finally, cessation of regeneration to avoid overgrowth or damage to nearby healthy tissue.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle of brain regeneration based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Production of new CNS cells has been a major focus in brain regeneration research.
source: Of these steps, production of new CNS cells has been a major focus.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the field, supported by the citations that follow.

claim: Mammalian stem cell-based approaches enabled the creation of new, often functional, neurons in vitro.
source: The advent of mammalian stem cell-based approaches and advances in cell reprogramming enabled the creation of new, often functional, neurons in vitro (Wichterle et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2001; Yan et al., 2005; Han et al., 2012; Vierbuchen et al., 2010; Elkabetz and Studer, 2008; Piña-Crespo et al., 2012; Wernig et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Advances in cell reprogramming enabled the creation of new, often functional, neurons in vitro.
source: The advent of mammalian stem cell-based approaches and advances in cell reprogramming enabled the creation of new, often functional, neurons in vitro (Wichterle et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2001; Yan et al., 2005; Han et al., 2012; Vierbuchen et al., 2010; Elkabetz and Studer, 2008; Piña-Crespo et al., 2012; Wernig et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Endogenous stem cell pools exist in the mammalian brain.
source: Additionally, the discovery of endogenous stem cell pools in the mammalian brain (Altman and Das, 1965; Eriksson et al., 1998) raises the possibility of enhancing the brain's ability to create new neurons from within (for a review of this progress, see Gage and Temple, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The discovery of endogenous stem cell pools in the mammalian brain raises the possibility of enhancing the brain's ability to create new neurons from within.
source: Additionally, the discovery of endogenous stem cell pools in the mammalian brain (Altman and Das, 1965; Eriksson et al., 1998) raises the possibility of enhancing the brain's ability to create new neurons from within (for a review of this progress, see Gage and Temple, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a logical inference from the discovery of stem cells, supported by citations.

claim: Functional repair in the human CNS remains an extremely ambitious goal.
source: Despite these advances, functional repair in the human CNS remains an extremely ambitious goal and requires the development of new therapies aimed not only at generation of new cells, but also placing and integrating these cells appropriately within a broader regenerative context.
evidence: This is stated as an assessment of the current state of the field based on established knowledge.

claim: Functional repair in the human CNS requires the development of new therapies aimed at generation of new cells and placing and integrating these cells appropriately within a broader regenerative context.
source: Despite these advances, functional repair in the human CNS remains an extremely ambitious goal and requires the development of new therapies aimed not only at generation of new cells, but also placing and integrating these cells appropriately within a broader regenerative context.
evidence: This is stated as an inference about what is needed for functional repair based on current knowledge.

claim: Zebrafish have a greater regenerative capacity than mammals.
source: While some species, like zebrafish and axolotls have a greater regenerative capacity than do mammals, species with the ability to regenerate an entire brain de novo are rare in the animal kingdom and in the realm of established model organisms (Bely and Nyberg, 2010; Tanaka and Ferretti, 2009; Egger et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Axolotls have a greater regenerative capacity than mammals.
source: While some species, like zebrafish and axolotls have a greater regenerative capacity than do mammals, species with the ability to regenerate an entire brain de novo are rare in the animal kingdom and in the realm of established model organisms (Bely and Nyberg, 2010; Tanaka and Ferretti, 2009; Egger et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Species with the ability to regenerate an entire brain de novo are rare in the animal kingdom.
source: While some species, like zebrafish and axolotls have a greater regenerative capacity than do mammals, species with the ability to regenerate an entire brain de novo are rare in the animal kingdom and in the realm of established model organisms (Bely and Nyberg, 2010; Tanaka and Ferretti, 2009; Egger et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Planarians have emerged as a tractable model system to study brain regeneration.
source: Of the small number of animals that regenerate their brains after injury, planarians have emerged as a tractable model system in which to study this remarkable process.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the field based on established knowledge.

claim: Scientists have appreciated the extreme capacity for regeneration found in planarians for over two hundred years.
source: Scientists have appreciated the extreme capacity for regeneration found in planarians for over two hundred years (Elliott and Sánchez Alvarado, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A nascent brain structure appears soon after amputation in planarians.
source: A nascent brain structure appears soon after amputation (Cebrià et al., 2002b) and reproducible brain wiring is indicated by full functional recovery, with resumed movement and feeding after one week (Inoue et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Reproducible brain wiring in planarians is indicated by full functional recovery, with resumed movement and feeding after one week.
source: A nascent brain structure appears soon after amputation (Cebrià et al., 2002b) and reproducible brain wiring is indicated by full functional recovery, with resumed movement and feeding after one week (Inoue et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The planarian CNS consists of bi-lobed cephalic ganglia (the brain) and two ventral nerve cords.
source: Anatomical studies have revealed details of the structure and molecular complexity of the planarian central nervous system (CNS), which consists of bi-lobed cephalic ganglia (the brain) and two ventral nerve cords (Figure 1A; Agata et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The planarian brain is composed of a diverse array of neural subtypes that produce conserved neurotransmitters and dozens of neuropeptides.
source: The planarian brain is composed of a diverse array of neural subtypes that produce conserved neurotransmitters and dozens of neuropeptides (Nishimura et al., 2007a, 2007b; 2008a; 2010; 2008b; Collins et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Neural cell types in the planarian brain are regionally organized.
source: These cell types are regionally organized, with subtypes of cells appearing medially or in lateral structures called brain branches that project toward the margin of the head (MacRae, 1967; Cebrià et al., 2002a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Brain branches are lateral structures that project toward the margin of the head in planarians.
source: These cell types are regionally organized, with subtypes of cells appearing medially or in lateral structures called brain branches that project toward the margin of the head (MacRae, 1967; Cebrià et al., 2002a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Planarians regenerate missing brain tissue regardless of the amputation plane or the severity of the injury to the CNS.
source: Planarians also regenerate missing brain tissue regardless of the amputation plane or the severity of the injury to the CNS (Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Over 900 transcripts were upregulated at one or more time points in regenerating animals compared to cut controls.
source: Over 900 transcripts were upregulated (≥2x, p≤0.01) at one or more time points in regenerating animals compared to cut (0 hr) controls that were initially identical to the regenerating animals (Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 1C.

claim: Approximately 45% of transcripts upregulated vs. cut controls at each time point were also upregulated vs. whole animals.
source: Furthermore, ~45% of transcripts upregulated vs. cut controls at each time point were also upregulated vs. whole animals (Figure 1D), indicating that differentially expressed genes do not simply reflect a return to homeostatic gene expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 1D.

claim: Differentially expressed genes during regeneration do not simply reflect a return to homeostatic gene expression.
source: Furthermore, ~45% of transcripts upregulated vs. cut controls at each time point were also upregulated vs. whole animals (Figure 1D), indicating that differentially expressed genes do not simply reflect a return to homeostatic gene expression.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the RNA-seq data showing that many upregulated genes are also upregulated compared to whole animals.

claim: 47% of upregulated genes with clear expression patterns showed enrichment in the CNS.
source: We hypothesized that our dataset would be enriched in genes expressed in the CNS and, indeed, found that 47% of genes with clear expression patterns showed enrichment in the CNS (170/362, Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 1F-G.

claim: Of the 170 genes with CNS expression, 132 were expressed broadly and 38 showed enrichment in subsets of CNS cells.
source: Of the 170 genes with CNS expression, 132 were expressed broadly and 38 showed enrichment in subsets of CNS cells (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 1F-G.

claim: 9% of upregulated genes with detectable expression patterns showed enriched expression in the head.
source: Of upregulated genes with detectable expression patterns, we also found that 9% showed enriched expression in the head (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–C) and 17% were expressed in the parenchyma, some in a pattern similar to neoblast genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–C.

claim: 17% of upregulated genes with detectable expression patterns were expressed in the parenchyma.
source: Of upregulated genes with detectable expression patterns, we also found that 9% showed enriched expression in the head (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–C) and 17% were expressed in the parenchyma, some in a pattern similar to neoblast genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–E.

claim: 9.2% (30/326) of screened genes caused a significant reduction in brain area after RNAi.
source: Of the genes screened, 9.2% (30/326) caused a significant reduction in brain area after RNAi (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi and in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 2C.

claim: sp6-9(RNAi) caused defects in eye regeneration.
source: RNAi targeting two additional genes caused nervous system regeneration phenotypes without a small brain (Supplementary file 3B): sp6-9(RNAi) caused defects in eye regeneration (Lapan and Reddien, 2011) and arrowhead(RNAi) caused defects at the midline of the brain which will be described below.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: arrowhead(RNAi) caused defects at the midline of the brain.
source: RNAi targeting two additional genes caused nervous system regeneration phenotypes without a small brain (Supplementary file 3B): sp6-9(RNAi) caused defects in eye regeneration (Lapan and Reddien, 2011) and arrowhead(RNAi) caused defects at the midline of the brain which will be described below.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data presented later in the manuscript.

claim: RNAi knockdown of 5 genes reduced sFRP-1 expression during regeneration.
source: RNAi knockdown of 5 genes (argininosuccinate synthase, autophagy-related 13, smarcb1, fzd-5/8–2, and hesl-3) reduced sFRP-1 expression during regeneration, with reductions ranging from minor to severe (Figure 2C-blue bars, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Knockdown of three genes caused a reduction in smedwi-1 signal: snRNPC, rbp-1-like, and soxP-1.
source: We determined that knockdown of three genes caused a reduction in smedwi-1 signal: snRNPC and rbp-1-like, which have not been described, and the previously identified gene soxP-1 (Figure 2C-red bars, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; Wagner et al., 2012; Wenemoser et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, as well as citations to prior work for soxP-1.

claim: RNAi of five genes caused smaller blastemas after regeneration.
source: RNAi of five genes (tRNA synthase, GTPbp, argininosuccinate synthase, wdr24, and smarcb1) caused smaller blastemas after regeneration and only GTPbp(RNAi) had an anterior-specific reduced blastema size (Supplementary file 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by blastema size measurements presented in Supplementary file 3B.

claim: Only GTPbp(RNAi) had an anterior-specific reduced blastema size.
source: RNAi of five genes (tRNA synthase, GTPbp, argininosuccinate synthase, wdr24, and smarcb1) caused smaller blastemas after regeneration and only GTPbp(RNAi) had an anterior-specific reduced blastema size (Supplementary file 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by blastema size measurements presented in Supplementary file 3B.

claim: soxB2-2 is expressed in cells of the head in whole animals.
source: soxB2-2 was expressed in cells of the head in whole animals (Figure 3A) and is expressed in a small number of cells in the anterior of regenerating planarians (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 3A.

claim: soxB2-2 is expressed in a small number of cells in the anterior of regenerating planarians.
source: soxB2-2 was expressed in cells of the head in whole animals (Figure 3A) and is expressed in a small number of cells in the anterior of regenerating planarians (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 3B.

claim: soxB2-2 was expressed in stem cells and stem cell progeny.
source: A prior transcriptomic study found that soxB2-2 was expressed in stem cells and stem cell progeny (Labbé et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: soxB2-2(RNAi) animals showed a small brain phenotype.
source: Importantly, soxB2-2(RNAi) animals showed a small brain phenotype (Figure 2B–C) and also a reduced response to vibrations in their environment (Videos 1–2).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization and brain area quantification data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 2B–C.

claim: soxB2-2(RNAi) animals showed a reduced response to vibrations in their environment.
source: Importantly, soxB2-2(RNAi) animals showed a small brain phenotype (Figure 2B–C) and also a reduced response to vibrations in their environment (Videos 1–2).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Videos 1–2.

claim: After soxB2-2(RNAi), tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) was significantly downregulated.
source: The only neural marker to be significantly downregulated after soxB2-2(RNAi) was tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) (Figure 3C), though loss of neural subsets (rather than whole classes) might be difficult to detect with this methodology.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 3C.

claim: Several neural progenitor genes were consistently downregulated after soxB2-2(RNAi), including significant downregulation of hlh-1, otxA, and POU2/3–2.
source: However, several neural progenitor genes were consistently downregulated after soxB2-2(RNAi), including significant downregulation of hlh-1, otxA, and POU2/3–2 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 3C.

claim: SoxB2-2 plays a role in promoting expression of a neural progenitor gene during the course of brain regeneration.
source: We therefore conclude that SoxB2-2 plays a role in promoting expression of a neural progenitor gene during the course of brain regeneration.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the qPCR and FISH data showing downregulation of neural progenitor genes after soxB2-2(RNAi).

claim: runt is expressed during homeostasis in the brain and during regeneration throughout the blastema.
source: Another gene required during brain regeneration is runt, which encodes a transcription factor expressed during homeostasis in the brain and during regeneration throughout the blastema (Figure 3D–E) in neoblasts and their progeny (Labbé et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 3D–E, as well as a citation to prior work.

claim: runt was previously identified as a wound-induced gene required for specification of sp6-9+ and AP2+ progenitors and for proper regeneration of cells of the planarian eye.
source: runt was previously identified as a wound-induced gene required for specification of sp6-9+and AP2+progenitors and for proper regeneration of cells of the planarian eye (Wenemoser et al., 2012; Sandmann et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Knockdown of runt leads to reduced levels of the neural progenitor markers ovo, glass, and klf.
source: We also found that knockdown of runt leads to reduced levels of the neural progenitor markers ovo, glass, and klf (Figure 3F), without influencing anterior fate or the broad expression of neural genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 3F.

claim: runt is important for directing expression of several neural progenitor genes that promote cell fates in the eye and beyond.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that runt is important for directing expression of several neural progenitor genes that promote cell fates in the eye (sp6-9+ and ovo) and beyond.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the qPCR data and prior work showing runt's role in eye regeneration.

claim: hesl-3 is expressed in presumptive neural progenitors and cells of the brain.
source: Like soxB2-2 and runt, the upregulated hes/hey-related gene, hesl-3, is also expressed in presumptive neural progenitors and cells of the brain (Cowles et al., 2013; Figure 3G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 3G–H, as well as a citation to prior work.

claim: hesl-3(RNAi) results in cyclopia and a small brain fused at the midline.
source: However, in contrast to soxB2-2 and runt, hesl-3(RNAi) results in cyclopia and a small brain fused at the midline (Cowles et al., 2013; Figure 2C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 2C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, as well as a citation to prior work.

claim: The primary effect of hesl-3(RNAi) was downregulation of anterior polarity markers sFRP-1 and foxD.
source: When we examined gene expression after hesl-3(RNAi), the primary effect we observed was downregulation of anterior polarity markers sFRP-1 and foxD (Figure 3I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR and in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 3I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: mblk is expressed in the brain branches of the planarian CNS.
source: One of these genes, mblk, is expressed in the brain branches of the planarian CNS (Figure 3J–K) and is related to the mushroom body large-type Kenyon cell-specific (mblk) gene, which encodes a putative transcription factor in honeybees (Takeuchi et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 3J–K.

claim: mblk is related to the mushroom body large-type Kenyon cell-specific (mblk) gene, which encodes a putative transcription factor in honeybees.
source: One of these genes, mblk, is expressed in the brain branches of the planarian CNS (Figure 3J–K) and is related to the mushroom body large-type Kenyon cell-specific (mblk) gene, which encodes a putative transcription factor in honeybees (Takeuchi et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: mblk is not expressed in neoblasts, but in neoblast progeny and differentiated cells.
source: mblk is not expressed in neoblasts, but in neoblast progeny and differentiated cells (Labbé et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: After mblk(RNAi), no changes in anterior genes or neural markers were observed, and progenitor genes were either unaffected or even upregulated.
source: After mblk(RNAi), we observed no changes in anterior genes or neural markers, and progenitor genes were either unaffected or even upregulated (Figure 3L).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 3L.

claim: CRELD encodes a putative secreted or transmembrane protein.
source: The second gene, CRELD (cysteine-rich egf-like domain), encodes a putative secreted or transmembrane protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) and is expressed in the planarian brain and head, with anterior upregulation in regenerating worms (Figure 3M–N).
evidence: This claim is supported by domain analysis data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: CRELD is expressed in the planarian brain and head, with anterior upregulation in regenerating worms.
source: The second gene, CRELD (cysteine-rich egf-like domain), encodes a putative secreted or transmembrane protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) and is expressed in the planarian brain and head, with anterior upregulation in regenerating worms (Figure 3M–N).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 3M–N.

claim: No changes in polarity markers, neural genes, or progenitor genes were detected after CRELD(RNAi).
source: We were unable to detect changes in polarity markers, neural genes, or progenitor genes after CRELD(RNAi) (Figure 3O), despite a small brain phenotype after this treatment (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 3O.

claim: LDLRR-1 and LDLRR-2 were previously identified in an analysis of wound-response genes.
source: One such group of genes is the LDLRR (low density lipoprotein receptor-related) family. LDLRR-1 and LDLRR-2 were previously identified in an analysis of wound-response genes (Wenemoser et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: LDLRR-1 is expressed in the parenchyma.
source: LDLRR-1 is expressed in the parenchyma, while LDLRR-2 is expressed in a subset of intestinal cells and in epithelial cells, particularly in the head (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 4A.

claim: LDLRR-2 is expressed in a subset of intestinal cells and in epithelial cells, particularly in the head.
source: LDLRR-1 is expressed in the parenchyma, while LDLRR-2 is expressed in a subset of intestinal cells and in epithelial cells, particularly in the head (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 4A.

claim: LDLRR-1 and LDLRR-2 show redistribution of expression after injury, with punctate expression in the blastema during regeneration.
source: Both show redistribution of expression after injury, with punctate expression in the blastema during regeneration (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 4A.

claim: LDLRR-3 is expressed in a pattern resembling that of LDLRR-1.
source: We also identified a gene with similarity to LDLRR-1 in our functional screen, which we have named LDLRR-3; this gene is also expressed in a pattern resembling that of LDLRR-1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 4A.

claim: LDLRR-1 is likely to be a secreted molecule or to remain attached to the cell surface by other means.
source: LDLRR-1 was so named for an LDLR (Low Density Lipoprotein Receptor) domain (Wenemoser et al., 2012); however, the current gene model for LDLRR-1 includes a signal peptide sequence but no transmembrane domain, suggesting that LDLRR-1 is likely to be a secreted molecule or to remain attached to the cell surface by other means (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on domain analysis data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: LDLRR-3 has a domain architecture similar to LDLRR-1 and also lacks a transmembrane domain.
source: We were unable to detect known domains within the existing LDLRR-2 sequence, but LDLRR-3 has a domain architecture similar to LDLRR-1 and also lacks a transmembrane domain (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by domain analysis data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 4B.

claim: LDLRR-1 and LDLRR-3 share closest similarity with proteins of the Heparan Sulfate Proteoglycan (HSPG) family.
source: Furthermore, LDLRR-1 and LDLRR-3 share closest similarity with proteins of the Heparan Sulfate Proteoglycan (HSPG) family (Supplementary file 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data presented in Supplementary file 3G.

claim: HSPGs play diverse roles in regulation of the extracellular matrix and signaling.
source: HSPGs play diverse roles in regulation of the extracellular matrix and signaling (for review, see Lin, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: LDLRR-3 is not irradiation sensitive.
source: LDLRR-3 is not irradiation sensitive (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A; Labbé et al., 2012) and we confirmed that LDLRR-3+ cells in the parenchyma are distinct from (but sometimes adjacent to) smedwi-1+ stem cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data after irradiation presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, as well as a citation to prior work.

claim: LDLRR-3+ cells in the parenchyma are distinct from (but sometimes adjacent to) smedwi-1+ stem cells.
source: LDLRR-3 is not irradiation sensitive (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A; Labbé et al., 2012) and we confirmed that LDLRR-3+ cells in the parenchyma are distinct from (but sometimes adjacent to) smedwi-1+ stem cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 4C.

claim: LDLRR-3+ cells do not express the muscle marker mhc.
source: Because muscle cells secrete position-control factors that set up the body axis of planarians (Witchley et al., 2013), we tested whether LDLRR-3 could be produced by muscle cells. We found that LDLRR-3+cells do not express the muscle marker mhc (myosin heavy chain; Figure 4C; Kobayashi et al., 1998); thus, LDLRR-3 is expressed in differentiated, non-muscle cells to promote regeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 4C.

claim: LDLRR-3 is expressed in differentiated, non-muscle cells to promote regeneration.
source: Because muscle cells secrete position-control factors that set up the body axis of planarians (Witchley et al., 2013), we tested whether LDLRR-3 could be produced by muscle cells. We found that LDLRR-3+cells do not express the muscle marker mhc (myosin heavy chain; Figure 4C; Kobayashi et al., 1998); thus, LDLRR-3 is expressed in differentiated, non-muscle cells to promote regeneration.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on FISH data showing LDLRR-3 is not expressed in muscle or stem cells.

claim: All LDLRR-3+ cells express LDLRR-1, but only half of LDLRR-1+ cells express LDLRR-3.
source: Furthermore, while LDLRR-1 and LDLRR-3 are expressed in similar patterns (Figure 4A), their expression is only partly overlapping (Figure 4C); all LDLRR-3+ cells express LDLRR-1, but only half of LDLRR-1+ cells express LDLRR-3.
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 4C.

claim: LDLRR-1 is also expressed in differentiated, mhc- cells.
source: As expected based on this finding, LDLRR-1 is also expressed in differentiated, mhc- cells (Figure 4C; Labbé et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 4C, as well as a citation to prior work.

claim: LDLRR-1 was identified as a wound response gene.
source: Because LDLRR-1 was identified as a wound response gene (Wenemoser et al., 2012), we examined other wound response genes (follistatin, jun, inhibin, and runt) in LDLRR-1(RNAi) and LDLRR-3(RNAi) animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: No diminished wound response was observed after LDLRR-1(RNAi) or LDLRR-3(RNAi).
source: Because LDLRR-1 was identified as a wound response gene (Wenemoser et al., 2012), we examined other wound response genes (follistatin, jun, inhibin, and runt) in LDLRR-1(RNAi) and LDLRR-3(RNAi) animals. We were not able to observe any diminished wound response after these perturbations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: Planarian F-spondin is expressed in parenchymal, differentiated cells that are not mhc+.
source: In addition to the LDLRR family, a gene encoding planarian F-spondin was identified as important for CNS regeneration in our functional screen. F-spondin is also expressed in parenchymal, differentiated cells that are not mhc+ (Figure 4A,C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization and FISH data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 4A, C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The predicted planarian F-spondin protein possesses a signal peptide but lacks a transmembrane domain.
source: Furthermore, the predicted planarian F-spondin protein possesses a signal peptide but lacks a transmembrane domain (Figure 4D), suggesting that it is secreted, like its homologs in other species (Feinstein and Klar, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by domain analysis data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 4D.

claim: Planarian F-spondin is likely secreted, like its homologs in other species.
source: Furthermore, the predicted planarian F-spondin protein possesses a signal peptide but lacks a transmembrane domain (Figure 4D), suggesting that it is secreted, like its homologs in other species (Feinstein and Klar, 2004).
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on domain analysis and a citation to prior work on F-spondin homologs.

claim: One or more parenchymal cell types produce cues (including planarian LDLRR and F-spondin proteins) that promote regeneration of the CNS and/or regeneration more generally.
source: We thus conclude that one or more parenchymal cell types produce cues (including planarian LDLRR and F-spondin proteins) that promote regeneration of the CNS and/or regeneration more generally.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the expression patterns and RNAi phenotypes of LDLRR and F-spondin genes.

claim: Planarian arrowhead is a homolog of arrowhead, a gene that encodes a LIM-homeodomain transcription factor.
source: However, we did detect a specific phenotype after targeting the planarian homolog of arrowhead, a gene that encodes a LIM-homeodomain transcription factor (Curtiss and Heilig, 1995, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on arrowhead in other species.

claim: Planarian arrowhead is expressed in neurons, at least some of which are ChAT+.
source: Planarian arrowhead is expressed in neurons, at least some of which are ChAT+ (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 5A–B.

claim: arrowhead(RNAi) animals regenerated with a gap between the lobes of the cephalic ganglia.
source: Despite normal brain size, arrowhead(RNAi) animals regenerated with a gap between the lobes of the cephalic ganglia (Figure 5C, arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 5C.

claim: The medial gap in arrowhead(RNAi) animals was more clearly visualized with an anti-synapsin antibody that stains the planarian neuropil.
source: The medial gap was more clearly visualized with an anti-synapsin antibody that stains the planarian neuropil, a region rich in axons, dendrites, and synapses (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 5D–E.

claim: The anterior commissure is the largest commissure in the planarian CNS and connects the two lobes of the cephalic ganglia.
source: The anterior commissure is the largest commissure in the planarian CNS and connects the two lobes of the cephalic ganglia (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as a fact about planarian anatomy, supported by reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Many axons cross the midline at the anterior commissure, including photoreceptor axons.
source: Many axons cross the midline at the anterior commissure, including photoreceptor axons (Agata et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Photoreceptor axons appeared frayed and/or failed to cross the midline in a majority of arrowhead(RNAi) animals.
source: We detected photoreceptor neurons using an anti-arrestin antibody (VC-1; Agata et al., 1998) and determined that photoreceptor axons appeared frayed and/or failed to cross the midline in a majority of arrowhead(RNAi) animals (Figure 5F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 5F–G.

claim: Failure of photoreceptor axons to cross at the anterior commissure was never detected after control(RNAi).
source: Failure of photoreceptor axons to cross at the anterior commissure was never detected after control(RNAi) (Figure 5F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 5F–G.

claim: slit is a factor previously shown to regulate axon guidance in planarians.
source: One factor previously shown to regulate axon guidance in planarians is slit (Cebrià et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Some arrowhead+ cells are slit+.
source: While some arrowhead+ cells are slit+, the overall slit expression pattern was unaffected after arrowhead(RNAi) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The overall slit expression pattern was unaffected after arrowhead(RNAi).
source: While some arrowhead+ cells are slit+, the overall slit expression pattern was unaffected after arrowhead(RNAi) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: arrowhead regulates cells or factors that drive reconnection of the planarian brain lobes and organization of newly regenerated axons at the anterior commissure.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that arrowhead regulates cells or factors that drive reconnection of the planarian brain lobes and organization of newly regenerated axons at the anterior commissure.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the arrowhead(RNAi) phenotype data.

claim: Planarian brain branches have been ascribed functions in mechanosensing and/or chemosensing.
source: Planarian brain branches have been ascribed functions in mechanosensing and/or chemosensing (Oviedo et al., 2003, Umesono et al., 1997, Nakazawa et al., 2003) and the auricles at the edge of the head of other planarian species have been shown to be important for chemosensory behavior (Koehler, 1932, Farnesi and Tei, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The auricles at the edge of the head of other planarian species have been shown to be important for chemosensory behavior.
source: Planarian brain branches have been ascribed functions in mechanosensing and/or chemosensing (Oviedo et al., 2003, Umesono et al., 1997, Nakazawa et al., 2003) and the auricles at the edge of the head of other planarian species have been shown to be important for chemosensory behavior (Koehler, 1932, Farnesi and Tei, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: CNG1 is expressed in regions at the very edge of the head.
source: We observed a particularly interesting expression pattern for CNG1, which was expressed in regions at the very edge of the head (Figure 6A–B), a location expected for cells serving in a sensory capacity.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 6A–B.

claim: CNG channels play important signaling roles in the retina and olfactory neurons of other organisms, being activated by cyclic nucleotides downstream of sensory signaling.
source: CNG channels play important signaling roles in the retina and olfactory neurons of other organisms, being activated by cyclic nucleotides (cyclic AMP or cyclic GMP) downstream of sensory signaling (Pifferi et al., 2006; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review and reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: FLI-1(RNAi) animals consistently showed significantly reduced completion of the maze-based feeding assay, compared to control(RNAi) animals.
source: FLI-1(RNAi) animals consistently showed significantly reduced completion of the maze-based feeding assay, compared to control(RNAi) animals (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral assay data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 6C.

claim: FLI-1 encodes an ETS-family transcription factor that is expressed in numerous cells of the planarian brain branches.
source: FLI-1 encodes an ETS-family transcription factor that is expressed in numerous cells of the planarian brain branches (Figure 6A,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 6A,D.

claim: A minority of FLI-1+ cells express ChAT or GluR1.
source: A minority of FLI-1+ cells express ChAT or GluR1 (Figure 6E, arrowheads), suggesting that the FLI-1+ population likely represents a heterogeneous population of neural cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 6E.

claim: The FLI-1+ population likely represents a heterogeneous population of neural cells.
source: A minority of FLI-1+ cells express ChAT or GluR1 (Figure 6E, arrowheads), suggesting that the FLI-1+ population likely represents a heterogeneous population of neural cells.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the FISH data showing partial overlap with ChAT and GluR1.

claim: The planarian brain branches play a role in chemosensory behavior.
source: Taken together, our findings: i) support a role for the planarian brain branches in chemosensory behavior and ii) suggest that FLI-1 is important for regeneration of some aspect of CNS structure or connectivity that restores chemosensory function during regeneration.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the behavioral assay data showing FLI-1(RNAi) animals have reduced chemosensory behavior.

claim: FLI-1 is important for regeneration of some aspect of CNS structure or connectivity that restores chemosensory function during regeneration.
source: Taken together, our findings: i) support a role for the planarian brain branches in chemosensory behavior and ii) suggest that FLI-1 is important for regeneration of some aspect of CNS structure or connectivity that restores chemosensory function during regeneration.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the behavioral assay data showing FLI-1(RNAi) animals have reduced chemosensory behavior.

claim: The planarian homolog of activin is downregulated during regeneration.
source: As proof of principle, we found that the planarian homolog of activin, an inhibitor of regeneration (Roberts-Galbraith and Newmark, 2013, Gavino et al., 2013), is downregulated during regeneration (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Supplementary file 1 and citations to prior work showing activin is an inhibitor of regeneration.

claim: 534 transcripts were downregulated during regeneration.
source: We identified 534 downregulated transcripts, with the number of downregulated genes increasing between 12 hr and 72 hr post-amputation (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 7A.

claim: The number of downregulated genes increased between 12 hr and 72 hr post-amputation.
source: We identified 534 downregulated transcripts, with the number of downregulated genes increasing between 12 hr and 72 hr post-amputation (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 7A.

claim: The most frequent expression patterns for downregulated genes were in the peripharyngeal secretory cells and the intestine (39% and 24%, respectively).
source: The most frequent expression patterns for these genes were in the peripharyngeal secretory cells and the intestine (39% and 24%, respectively, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C), suggesting that cell loss or a change in the physiology of these organ systems occurs during the early stages of planarian head regeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Cell loss or a change in the physiology of the peripharyngeal secretory cells and intestine occurs during the early stages of planarian head regeneration.
source: The most frequent expression patterns for these genes were in the peripharyngeal secretory cells and the intestine (39% and 24%, respectively, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C), suggesting that cell loss or a change in the physiology of these organ systems occurs during the early stages of planarian head regeneration.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the high proportion of downregulated genes expressed in these tissues.

claim: 8/58 downregulated genes were expressed in the CNS (14%).
source: We also detected a number of genes expressed in posterior regions (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D), an expected pattern as posterior genes likely need to be downregulated after amputation to permit rescaling of the body axis. Ultimately, we determined that 8/58 genes were expressed in the CNS (14%, Figure 7B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 7B–C.

claim: The proportion of downregulated genes expressed in the CNS was about one third that of CNS expression patterns in the upregulated gene dataset.
source: Ultimately, we determined that 8/58 genes were expressed in the CNS (14%, Figure 7B–C). This proportion was about one third that of CNS expression patterns in the upregulated gene dataset.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between the proportions of CNS-expressed genes in the upregulated and downregulated datasets.

claim: IF-1 is expressed in the CNS in a pattern similar to antibody markers of the neuropil.
source: Of the downregulated genes expressed in the planarian CNS, one expression pattern was distinct. Expression of an intermediate filament gene (IF-1) was detected in the CNS in a pattern similar to antibody markers of the neuropil and different than neural gene expression, which typically marks cell bodies around the CNS (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 7C.

claim: IF-1 was expressed in cells present in the neuropil that did not express neural markers.
source: To test this possibility, we examined whether IF-1 was coexpressed with markers of abundant neural types, including PC-2 and ChAT. Indeed, IF-1 was expressed in cells present in the neuropil that did not express neural markers (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The existence of glial cells in planarians has been a matter of debate.
source: The nervous systems of many metazoans contain non-neural support cells that are broadly called glia. The existence of glial cells in planarians has been a matter of debate: electron microscopy analyses have been used to argue both for and against the presence of such cells (Morita and Best, 1966, Lentz, 1967, Baguñà and Ballester, 1978, Golubev, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work with conflicting conclusions.

claim: IF-1 shares some similarity with intermediate filament genes expressed in neurons and glia.
source: IF-1 itself shares some similarity with intermediate filament genes expressed in neurons (vertebrate neurofilament and C. elegans intermediate filament, ifa-1) and glia (vertebrate glial fibrillary acid protein) (Supplementary file 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data presented in Supplementary file 3G.

claim: Astrocytes take up glutamate and convert it to glutamine.
source: One frequent function of glial cells is to take up excess neurotransmitters or other chemicals that can be toxic to nearby neurons. For example, astrocytes take up glutamate and convert it to glutamine (Schousboe et al., 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Glutamate uptake occurs through excitatory amino acid transporters and conversion of glutamate to glutamine is catalyzed by glutamine synthetase.
source: Glutamate uptake occurs through excitatory amino acid transporters and conversion of glutamate to glutamine is catalyzed by glutamine synthetase (Rothstein et al., 1994, Norenberg and Martinez-Hernandez, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Planarian slc1a-5 and GS-1 were expressed in a pattern similar to IF-1.
source: We therefore investigated the expression patterns of planarian slc1a-5 (solute carrier 1a-5 / EAAT) and GS-1 (glutamine synthetase-1) and found that they were also expressed in a pattern similar to IF-1 (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 8B.

claim: IF-1 is coexpressed with both slc1a-5 and GS-1.
source: Furthermore, we detected IF-1 coexpression with both slc1a-5 and GS-1 (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 8C.

claim: Many of the genes coexpressed with IF-1 are not differentially expressed or are even slightly upregulated during regeneration.
source: Importantly, many of the genes coexpressed with IF-1 are not differentially expressed (slc1a-5 and slc6a-2) or are even slightly upregulated during regeneration (slc2a-1, GS-1, and slc7a-8).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: IF-1+ glial cells in planarians are similar to glial cells (and in particular astrocytes) in other organisms, in that they express a variety of transporters of the solute carrier family.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that IF-1+ glial cells in planarians are similar to glial cells (and in particular astrocytes) in other organisms, in that they express a variety of transporters of the solute carrier family (Cahoy et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the FISH data showing coexpression of IF-1 with solute carrier genes, supported by a citation to prior work on glial gene expression.

claim: Glial cells are not lost after injury, but instead alter their gene expression.
source: Furthermore, because most markers coexpressed with IF-1 are not reduced after amputation, we conclude that glial cells are not lost after injury, but instead alter their gene expression.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the observation that most glial markers are not downregulated after injury.

claim: Two transcripts from module 2 were expressed in IF-1+ cells: jagged-like and estrella.
source: As a pilot study, we cloned 48 genes from this module and examined their expression patterns. The majority of these genes showed expression patterns irrelevant to our glial studies. However, two transcripts were expressed in IF-1+cells (Figure 8D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 8D–E.

claim: jagged-like encodes a protein with weak similarity to Jagged that contains a signal peptide, two EGF domains, and a transmembrane domain.
source: jagged-like encodes a protein with weak similarity to Jagged that contains a signal peptide, two EGF domains, and a transmembrane domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by domain analysis data.

claim: estrella encodes a signal peptide-containing protein.
source: We also identified a gene that encodes a signal peptide-containing protein; we named this novel gene estrella ('star' in Catalan) based on its expression pattern and the origin of our S. mediterranea strain in Barcelona.
evidence: This claim is supported by domain analysis data.

claim: The expression pattern of estrella highlights the extensive processes of glial cells and their wide distribution in the neuropil, the peripheral nervous system, near the brain branches, and near photoreceptors.
source: The expression pattern of estrella highlights the extensive processes of glial cells and their wide distribution in the neuropil, the peripheral nervous system, near the brain branches, and near photoreceptors (Figure 8F–G; Cowles et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 8F–G.

claim: IF-1+ glial cells respond to injury by downregulating a variety of genes (including genes that encode potential signaling molecules) over the course of several days.
source: Together, our results indicate that IF-1+ glial cells respond to injury by downregulating a variety of genes (including genes that encode potential signaling molecules) over the course of several days.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the RNA-seq and FISH data showing downregulation of IF-1, jagged-like, and estrella after injury.

claim: Cells in the neuropil were detected that had numerous fine cellular processes that intermingled with axons.
source: Finally, we used electron microscopy to confirm the existence of glial cells in the planarian neuropil. Indeed, we detected cells in the neuropil that had numerous fine cellular processes that intermingled with axons (Figure 8H–I, Video 3–4).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 8H–I and Videos 3–4.

claim: Planarian glial cells were distinct from nearby neurons in that they had electron-dense cytoplasm and elongated nuclei with abundant peripheral heterochromatin.
source: Planarian glial cells were also distinct from nearby neurons in that they had electron-dense cytoplasm and elongated nuclei with abundant peripheral heterochromatin (Figure 8H).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 8H.

claim: Electron-dense projections were common throughout the neuropil, suggesting extensive projection of glial cells throughout the neuropil of the planarian nervous system.
source: Throughout the neuropil, where neuronal processes are a dominant feature, electron-dense projections were also common (Video 5), suggesting extensive projection of glial cells throughout the neuropil of the planarian nervous system.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on electron microscopy data presented in Video 5.

claim: Both gene expression data and electron microscopic analysis support the existence of glia in the planarian CNS.
source: We therefore conclude that both our gene expression data and electron microscopic analysis support the existence of glia in the planarian CNS.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the combined gene expression and electron microscopy data.

claim: Muscle cells produce polarity cues during homeostasis and in response to injury.
source: While muscle cells produce polarity cues during homeostasis and in response to injury (Wurtzel et al., 2015; Witchley et al., 2013), it is not yet clear whether they also produce molecules that promote regeneration, or whether other cells carry out or assist in this key signaling role.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: It is not yet clear whether muscle cells produce molecules that promote regeneration, or whether other cells carry out or assist in this key signaling role.
source: While muscle cells produce polarity cues during homeostasis and in response to injury (Wurtzel et al., 2015; Witchley et al., 2013), it is not yet clear whether they also produce molecules that promote regeneration, or whether other cells carry out or assist in this key signaling role.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Planarian regenerative ability depends on a pool of stem cells called neoblasts, at least some of which are pluripotent.
source: The regenerative ability of planarians depends on a pool of stem cells called neoblasts, at least some of which are pluripotent (Wagner et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The planarian stem cell pool is heterogeneous.
source: This stem cell pool is heterogeneous (van Wolfswinkel et al., 2014; Moritz et al., 2012; Hayashi et al., 2010) and stem cells respond to injury by migrating, proliferating, and producing daughter cells that differentiate to replace all cell types of the body (Saló and Baguñà, 1985; Baguñà et al., 1989; Baguñà, 1976).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Stem cells respond to injury by migrating, proliferating, and producing daughter cells that differentiate to replace all cell types of the body.
source: This stem cell pool is heterogeneous (van Wolfswinkel et al., 2014; Moritz et al., 2012; Hayashi et al., 2010) and stem cells respond to injury by migrating, proliferating, and producing daughter cells that differentiate to replace all cell types of the body (Saló and Baguñà, 1985; Baguñà et al., 1989; Baguñà, 1976).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Planarians restore their axial polarity after injury.
source: Additionally, planarians restore their axial polarity after injury; polarity markers reappear early during the regenerative process and are responsible for resetting the body plan (reviewed in Adell et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: Polarity markers reappear early during the regenerative process and are responsible for resetting the body plan.
source: Additionally, planarians restore their axial polarity after injury; polarity markers reappear early during the regenerative process and are responsible for resetting the body plan (reviewed in Adell et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: Anterior cues (including Notum and secreted Frizzled-related proteins) inhibit posterior Wnt ligands to enable head and brain regeneration.
source: Specifically, anterior cues (including Notum and secreted Frizzled-related proteins) inhibit posterior Wnt ligands to enable head and brain regeneration (Petersen and Reddien, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Several regulators of planarian brain regeneration were uncovered through candidate-gene approaches, including axon guidance cues like Slit/Robo and Netrin/DCC as well as transcriptional regulators of certain neural subtypes, including Lhx1/5–1, Coe, and others.
source: Several regulators of planarian brain regeneration were uncovered through candidate-gene approaches, including axon guidance cues like Slit/Robo and Netrin/DCC as well as transcriptional regulators of certain neural subtypes, including Lhx1/5–1, Coe, and others (Cebrià and Newmark, 2005, 2007; Cebrià et al., 2007; Currie and Pearson, 2013; Cowles et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.
